rv.q: In Pippa Nixon's Beatrice and Ken Nwosu's Benedick, it gives us one of the most charming accounts of Shakespeare's sparring partners this decade.

The cast is universally adept, particularly Nixon as the witty and stridently single Beatrice. She makes her part more tartly outraged by Benedick but still physically playful. Nwosu is a softer-edged Benedick with great comic timing, inflecting his lines with arch asides.
Chelsea Walker's Much Ado is a triumphant joy. She does not ignore the play's dark sides but works intelligently through them in a way that is satisfying and enlightening.
Walker brings wit, incisiveness and vigour to a play shot through with those very qualities.
This version is hugely enjoyable, even if some of the darker intent doesn't quite pack the punch that it could.

One outstanding moment includes Benedick tucking himself in with the audience groundlings, using their theatre programmes to hide his face as some of the play’s other characters gossip about him. Composed by Angus MacRae, there is a clever use of music throughout this production of Much Ado About Nothing.
There's a sense here of scenes from multiple productions spliced together, as though there's a more developed, more coherent version of Much Ado still waiting to be unearthed.
